opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, the tumor you can see is often not the whole story. By the time someone is diagnosed, there may already be microscopic cells that have escaped the primary site, things that won't show up on any scan. If you go straight to surgery, you've removed the visible mass, but those hidden cells are still there, and recovery from a big operation can delay systemic treatment by weeks or even months. Giving chemotherapy or immunotherapy first, what we call neoadjuvant therapy, starts treating the whole body right away.

There are a few other practical benefits too. Shrinking the tumor beforehand can make the surgery itself less extensive. Sometimes a tumor that was borderline resectable becomes cleanly removable, or a patient can keep more of an organ, like breast-conserving surgery instead of a mastectomy. With immunotherapy in particular, there's an interesting argument that having the tumor still in place helps. It acts as a source of antigens, so the immune system gets primed against the cancer while there's plenty to recognize, and that response can then hunt down residual disease after surgery.

And then, from my perspective as someone who works with data, one of the most valuable aspects is that it gives you an in vivo test of whether the treatment is working. When the surgeon removes the tumor, the pathologist can look at how much viable cancer is left. A complete pathologic response is a strong signal about prognosis, and if the response is poor, that tells you to change course afterward. So you're not just treating the patient, you're learning about their specific cancer's biology, and that's exactly the kind of information we'd love to feed into models that predict who will benefit from which therapy.

r001.rationale: The response says microscopic cells may have escaped the primary site and will not show up on scans.

r002.rationale: It explains that treatment before surgery starts treating the whole body, addressing the hidden cells that surgery would leave behind.

r003.rationale: The response mentions treating residual disease after surgery but does not say this may prevent cancer recurrence.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The intuition most people have is that if you can see a tumor, you should take it out as fast as possible, and historically that's how surgery was practiced. But over the last couple of decades we've learned that for a lot of cancers, the thing that actually kills people isn't the visible tumor, it's the microscopic disease we can't see, the cells that have already left the primary site and are sitting in the liver, the lungs, the peritoneum, wherever.

So the rationale for giving systemic therapy first, what we call neoadjuvant therapy, is really a few things layered on top of each other.

The first is that you treat that invisible disease right away, at a point when the patient is still strong, rather than waiting until they've recovered from a big operation, which can be eight or twelve weeks later and sometimes longer if there are complications. Some patients never get to their adjuvant chemo after surgery because they don't recover well enough. Giving it up front guarantees they get it.

The second is that it's essentially a biological test. You give a few cycles of treatment and then you re-image, and you watch what the tumor does. If it shrinks or stays stable, that tells you the biology is favorable and surgery is probably going to help. If it grows, or if new lesions show up while the patient is on treatment, that's the cancer telling you it was going to metastasize anyway, and a big operation would have been morbidity without benefit. You've spared that patient a surgery that wasn't going to cure them.

And the third is more practical: shrinking the tumor can make the operation itself easier and more likely to be complete, with clean margins, especially around vessels in something like pancreatic cancer.

Where this gets interesting from my side, in imaging and computational work, is that second point. We're really not very good at reading response on a CT scan. We measure diameters, and a tumor that's dying can look the same size as one that isn't, because it's being replaced by scar tissue. So a lot of what we do is try to pull more out of those images, texture, changes in enhancement, patterns across the whole tumor rather than one dimension, to figure out earlier and more reliably who is actually responding. Because that decision about whether to go ahead with surgery is one of the biggest decisions a patient will face, and right now we're making it with fairly crude tools.

r001.rationale: The response says the visible tumor can coexist with microscopic cells that have left the primary site and are in places such as the liver or lungs.

r002.rationale: It explains that systemic therapy given first treats this invisible disease throughout the body.

r003.rationale: The response discusses metastatic disease and whether surgery would help, but does not explain that eliminating undetected cells may prevent cancer recurrence.

astra-6.text:
The idea is that the tumor we can see may not be the whole disease. There may already be microscopic cancer cells elsewhere in the body that we can’t detect on a scan. Giving treatment before surgery—what we call neoadjuvant therapy—can start treating those cells and may shrink the tumor, making it easier to remove.

It also gives us a chance to see how the cancer responds. With immunotherapy, there’s an additional rationale: while the tumor is still present, it can provide a source of targets for the immune system to recognize, potentially helping it attack cancer cells elsewhere as well.

That doesn’t mean it’s the right approach for every patient. The benefit depends on the type and stage of cancer, and we have to weigh it against side effects and the risks of delaying surgery.

r001.rationale: It says the visible tumor may not be the whole disease and that microscopic cancer cells may already be elsewhere in the body, undetectable on a scan.

r002.rationale: It says pre-surgery treatment can start treating those cells, but does not clearly state that its aim is to destroy undetected cancer cells throughout the body.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that eliminating undetected cancer cells may prevent recurrence.

The visible tumor may not be the whole disease. Cancer cells can escape and spread elsewhere in the body before we can detect them on a scan. So giving treatment before surgery—what we call neoadjuvant therapy—can address those microscopic deposits while also shrinking the primary tumor, potentially making it easier to remove.

It also gives us a chance to see how the cancer responds. With immunotherapy, there’s an additional rationale: while the tumor is still present, it can provide a source of targets for the immune system to recognize, potentially helping it attack cancer cells elsewhere. Whether that approach makes sense depends on the cancer type, its stage, and the evidence for that treatment.
